subtopic: Statement versus open sentence versus command, question, exclamation
concept_tested: Recognising a declarative sentence that carries a definite truth value
stem: Which of the following sentences is a statement in logic?

options.A: Please shut the door of the classroom.
options.B: What is the square root of $16$?

distractor_rationale.A: Imperative sentence; the student accepts any grammatically complete sentence as a statement.
distractor_rationale.B: Interrogative sentence; the student thinks a sentence about mathematics is automatically a statement.
distractor_rationale.C: Open sentence; the student thinks an equation always has a definite truth value.

solution: A command, a question and an exclamation carry no truth value, so none of them is a statement. An equation in an unspecified variable $x$ is an open sentence; it becomes true or false only after $x$ is fixed. The sentence $\sqrt{16}$ is an irrational number is declarative and its truth value is $\mathbf{F}$, since $\sqrt{16} = 4$ is rational. A false declarative sentence is still a statement.
formula_principle: A statement is a declarative sentence whose truth value is exactly one of $\mathbf{T}$ or $\mathbf{F}$.
common_misconception: The student believes a sentence must be true to qualify as a statement, and rejects a false declarative sentence.

concept_tested: Separating an open sentence from a genuine statement
stem: Which of the following is an open sentence and not a statement?

options.A: Every prime number greater than $2$ is an odd number.
options.B: The equation $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has no real root.
options.D: $3$ is a root of the equation $x^2 - 9 = 0$.

concept_tested: Propagating the truth values of two simple statements through four connectives
stem: Let $p$: $7$ is a prime number, and $q$: $0$ is a positive integer. The truth values of $p \wedge q$, $p \vee q$, $p \rightarrow q$ and $p \leftrightarrow q$, in that order, are

distractor_rationale.A: The student thinks a conditional with a true antecedent and a false consequent is true.
distractor_rationale.C: The student requires both components to be true for a disjunction.
distractor_rationale.D: The student assigns truth value $\mathbf{T}$ to $q$, believing $0$ to be positive.

solution: The statement $p$ is true since $7$ has exactly two divisors. The statement $q$ is false since $0$ is neither positive nor negative. With $p$ true and $q$ false: $p \wedge q$ needs both true, so it is $\mathbf{F}$; $p \vee q$ needs at least one true, so it is $\mathbf{T}$; $p \rightarrow q$ has a true antecedent and a false consequent, the only false row of the conditional, so it is $\mathbf{F}$; $p \leftrightarrow q$ needs equal truth values, so it is $\mathbf{F}$.

common_misconception: The student forgets that the single false row of a conditional is exactly antecedent true with consequent false.

stem: Let $p$: $2$ is an even number, $q$: $\sqrt{9} = -3$, and $r$: $-5 < -2$. Which of the following compound statements is false?

subtopic: Conditional, its truth table, and the vacuous truth row
concept_tested: Deducing what must hold from the truth values of a conjunction and a conditional
stem: For two statements $p$ and $q$ it is given that $p \wedge q$ is false and $p \rightarrow q$ is true. Which of the following must then be true?

distractor_rationale.B: The student keeps only the surviving row in which $q$ is true and drops the other one.
distractor_rationale.C: The student keeps only the surviving row in which $q$ is false and drops the other one.
distractor_rationale.D: The student overlooks the row in which $p$ and $q$ are both false.

solution: Test the four rows. In the row $p$ true and $q$ true, $p \wedge q$ is true, which is not allowed. In the row $p$ true and $q$ false, $p \rightarrow q$ is false, which is not allowed. In the row $p$ false and $q$ true, $p \wedge q$ is false and $p \rightarrow q$ is true, so this row survives. In the row $p$ false and $q$ false, $p \wedge q$ is false and $p \rightarrow q$ is true, so this row survives too. In both surviving rows $p$ is false, so $\sim p$ is true in every case. In one surviving row $q$ is true and in the other $q$ is false, so neither $q$ nor $\sim q$ is forced; and $p \vee q$ is true in the first surviving row but false in the second, so it is not forced either.
formula_principle: Eliminate the rows of the two variable table that contradict the given truth values, then read what is common to the rows that survive.
common_misconception: The student picks the first row that fits the data instead of keeping every row that fits and reporting only what holds in all of them.

subtopic: Biconditional and its truth table
concept_tested: Stating the truth condition of the biconditional
stem: The biconditional $p \leftrightarrow q$ is true

options.A: only when $p$ and $q$ have different truth values
options.B: only when both $p$ and $q$ are true
options.C: only when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value
options.D: only when at least one of $p$ and $q$ is true

correct_answer_text: only when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value

distractor_rationale.B: The student drops the row in which both parts are false.
distractor_rationale.D: The student states the rule for inclusive disjunction.

formula_principle: $p \leftrightarrow q$ is $\mathbf{T}$ exactly in the two rows where $p$ and $q$ carry the same truth value.
common_misconception: The student remembers only the row where both parts are true and forgets that two false parts also give a true biconditional.

stem: In the truth table of $(p \leftrightarrow q) \rightarrow (p \wedge q)$, the number of rows carrying the entry $\mathbf{F}$ in the last column is

distractor_rationale.C: The student treats the pattern as a tautology.

concept_tested: Stating the truth condition of exclusive disjunction
stem: The exclusive disjunction $p \veebar q$ is true

options.A: only when exactly one of $p$ and $q$ is true
options.B: only when both $p$ and $q$ are true
options.C: only when at least one of $p$ and $q$ is true
options.D: only when both $p$ and $q$ are false

distractor_rationale.C: The student states the rule for inclusive disjunction.

common_misconception: The student treats $\veebar$ as the ordinary disjunction and marks the first row true as well.

concept_tested: Identifying the pattern whose truth column matches exclusive disjunction
stem: Which of the following statement patterns has exactly the same last column as $(p \wedge q) \rightarrow r$?

distractor_rationale.A: The student distributes the conditional over the conjunction as though it behaved like a disjunction in the antecedent.
distractor_rationale.B: The student writes the negation of the given pattern.
distractor_rationale.C: The student interchanges the antecedent and the consequent.

solution: Write the given pattern as $\sim (p \wedge q) \vee r$. By De Morgan's law $\sim (p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$, so the pattern is $\sim p \vee \sim q \vee r$. subtopic: Translating a verbal compound statement into symbolic form
concept_tested: Translating the phrase only if into a conditional in the correct direction
stem: Let $p$: Sunil is rich, and $q$: Sunil is happy. The symbolic form of the statement 'Sunil is happy only if he is rich' is

distractor_rationale.A: The student reads only if in the same direction as if, and reverses the conditional.
distractor_rationale.B: The student reads only if as if and only if.
distractor_rationale.D: The student turns only if into a negated antecedent.

solution: In $a$ only if $b$, the clause $b$ states a condition without which $a$ cannot hold, so $a$ forces $b$ and the arrow runs from $a$ to $b$. Here $a$ is Sunil is happy, which is $q$, and $b$ is he is rich, which is $p$. Hence the symbolic form is $q \rightarrow p$.
formula_principle: The sentence $a$ only if $b$ translates as $a \rightarrow b$, whereas $a$ if $b$ translates as $b \rightarrow a$.
common_misconception: The student treats only if exactly like if and writes the conditional the wrong way round.

concept_tested: Translating the construction neither nor
stem: Let $p$: Ravi passed the test, and $q$: Ramesh passed the test. The symbolic form of the statement 'Neither Ravi nor Ramesh passed the test' is

distractor_rationale.D: The student reads nor as a claim that the two results differ.

The first denial is $\sim p$, the second is $\sim q$, and the sentence asserts them together, so the connective is $\wedge$. Hence the symbolic form is $\sim p \wedge \sim q$. concept_tested: Translating the connective unless
stem: Let $p$: The picnic will be held, and $q$: It rains. The symbolic form of the statement 'The picnic will be held unless it rains' is

distractor_rationale.A: The student drops the negation that unless carries.
distractor_rationale.B: The student makes the picnic the antecedent instead of the weather.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads unless as if it simply joined the two parts in the order in which they appear.

solution: The word unless carries the sense if not. The sentence therefore says that if it does not rain then the picnic will be held, which is $\sim q \rightarrow p$. Note that the sentence promises nothing at all about what happens when it does rain, so it does not say $q \rightarrow \sim p$; in the row $q$ true and $p$ true, $\sim q \rightarrow p$ is $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$ while $q \rightarrow \sim p$ is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$, so the two are different patterns.
formula_principle: The sentence $a$ unless $b$ means if $b$ does not happen then $a$ happens, that is $\sim b \rightarrow a$.
common_misconception: The student reads unless as a two way promise and concludes that rain must cancel the picnic.

stem: Let $p$: It rains, $q$: The match is played, and $r$: The ground is wet. The symbolic form of the statement 'If it rains and the ground is wet, then the match is not played' is

concept_tested: Reading an exclusive disjunction of two switch statements in words
stem: Let $p$: The switch $S_1$ is closed, and $q$: The switch $S_2$ is closed. The verbal form of $p \veebar q$ is

options.A: Either the switch $S_1$ is closed or the switch $S_2$ is closed, but not both.
options.B: The switch $S_1$ is closed or the switch $S_2$ is closed, or both are closed.
options.C: The switch $S_1$ is closed as well as the switch $S_2$ is closed.
options.D: Neither the switch $S_1$ nor the switch $S_2$ is closed.

correct_answer_text: Either the switch $S_1$ is closed or the switch $S_2$ is closed, but not both.

distractor_rationale.B: The student reads $\veebar$ as the inclusive disjunction.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads $\veebar$ as a conjunction.
distractor_rationale.D: The student reads the bar under the symbol as a negation of the whole disjunction.

solution: The symbol $\veebar$ denotes exclusive disjunction, which is true exactly when one of the two parts is true and the other is false. In words this is either the switch $S_1$ is closed or the switch $S_2$ is closed, but not both. Dropping the clause but not both would give the inclusive disjunction $p \vee q$, which is a different pattern because it is also true when both switches are closed.
formula_principle: $p \veebar q$ is read as either $p$ or $q$ but not both.
common_misconception: The student ignores the bar in $\veebar$ and reads the symbol as the ordinary or.

subtopic: Translating a symbolic statement pattern into words
concept_tested: Reading a biconditional whose second side is itself a conjunction
stem: Let $p$: The number is divisible by $6$, $q$: The number is divisible by $2$, and $r$: The number is divisible by $3$. The verbal form of $p \leftrightarrow (q \wedge r)$ is

options.A: The number is divisible by $6$ if and only if it is divisible by $2$ or by $3$.
options.B: If the number is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$, then it is divisible by $6$.
options.C: If the number is divisible by $6$, then it is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$.
options.D: The number is divisible by $6$ if and only if it is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$.

correct_answer_text: The number is divisible by $6$ if and only if it is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$.

distractor_rationale.A: The student reads the inner conjunction as a disjunction.
distractor_rationale.B: The student reads the double arrow as a single arrow pointing left.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads the double arrow as a single arrow pointing right.

solution: The outer connective is $\leftrightarrow$, which is read as if and only if, so the sentence must contain that phrase and not a one way if then. The left side is $p$, the number is divisible by $6$. The right side is $q \wedge r$, that is the number is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$. Putting these together gives: the number is divisible by $6$ if and only if it is divisible by $2$ as well as by $3$.
formula_principle: $a \leftrightarrow b$ is read as $a$ if and only if $b$, and $\wedge$ inside a bracket is read as as well as.
common_misconception: The student weakens a biconditional to a one way conditional and loses half of the claim.

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in two variables
concept_tested: Producing the final column of a conjunction of two opposite conditionals
stem: The last column of the truth table of $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge (q \rightarrow p)$, taken for the assignments $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F})$ of $(p, q)$ in that order, is

distractor_rationale.A: The student assumes a conjunction of two conditionals is always true.
distractor_rationale.B: The student rejects the row in which $p$ and $q$ are both false.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads the pattern as an exclusive disjunction.

solution: The working table is $$\begin{array}{cc|ccc} p & q & p \rightarrow q & q \rightarrow p & (p \rightarrow q) \wedge (q \rightarrow p) \\ \hline \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} \end{array}$$ The last column reads $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$ downwards.
formula_principle: Build the two conditional columns separately, then take their conjunction row by row.
common_misconception: The student assumes that reversing the arrow cannot change a column and copies the same values into both conditional columns.

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in two variables
concept_tested: Completing a supplied two variable table for a conditional with a negated consequent
stem: The entries of the last column of the table below, read downwards, are $$\begin{array}{cc|c} p & q & p \rightarrow \sim q \\ \hline \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & ? \\ \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} & ? \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & ? \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} & ? \end{array}$$

distractor_rationale.A: The student copies the column of $\sim q$ instead of evaluating the conditional.
distractor_rationale.C: The student forgets the tilde and builds the column of $p \rightarrow q$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student marks the conditional false whenever $\sim q$ is false, regardless of $p$.

solution: The column of $\sim q$ is $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$. Row one gives $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$. Row two gives $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$. Row three gives $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{T}$, which is the vacuous truth row. Row four gives $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$. Reading downwards the column is $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$.
formula_principle: First write the column of $\sim q$, then apply the conditional rule using $p$ as antecedent.
common_misconception: The student reports the column of the negated consequent as though it were the column of the whole conditional.

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in two variables
concept_tested: Counting the true rows of a conjunction of two disjunctions
stem: In the truth table of $(\sim p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee \sim q)$, the number of rows carrying the entry $\mathbf{T}$ in the last column is

distractor_rationale.B: The student keeps only the row in which $p$ and $q$ are both true.
distractor_rationale.C: The student counts the true rows of a single disjunction.
distractor_rationale.D: The student assumes the pattern is a tautology.

solution: The working table is $$\begin{array}{cc|ccc} p & q & \sim p \vee q & p \vee \sim q & (\sim p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee \sim q) \\ \hline \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} & \mathbf{T} \end{array}$$ Two rows carry $\mathbf{T}$, namely the first and the last.
formula_principle: Build each disjunction column, then take the conjunction row by row and count the entries $\mathbf{T}$.
common_misconception: The student counts the true entries of one bracket and never combines the two brackets row by row.

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in two variables
concept_tested: Recovering the pattern from a given final truth column
stem: Which of the following statement patterns has the last column $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}$ for the assignments $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F})$ of $(p, q)$ in that order?

distractor_rationale.A: The student matches a column that is exactly the reverse of the required one.
distractor_rationale.B: The student matches only the first row and stops.
distractor_rationale.D: The student matches the second row and assumes the rest follows.

solution: For the four assignments in the stated order the columns are: $p \veebar q$ gives $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}$; $p \leftrightarrow q$ gives $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$; $\sim(p \vee q)$ gives $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$; and $p \wedge \sim q$ gives $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}$. Only the first column matches the required $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}$. Note that the required column is true exactly when the two truth values differ, which is the description of exclusive disjunction.
formula_principle: A pattern is determined by its final column, so build all four candidate columns and compare them entry by entry.
common_misconception: The student stops comparing after the first agreeing row instead of checking all four rows.

concept_tested: Fixing the number of rows of a truth table from the number of statements
stem: The number of rows in the truth table of a statement pattern built from the three statements $p$, $q$ and $r$ is

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in three variables
concept_tested: Counting the true rows of a disjunction whose first part is a conjunction
stem: For how many of the eight rows of its truth table is the statement pattern $(p \wedge q) \vee r$ true?

distractor_rationale.B: The student counts only the rows in which $r$ is true.
distractor_rationale.C: The student double counts the two rows in which $p \wedge q$ and $r$ are both true.
distractor_rationale.D: The student requires $p \wedge q$ to be true as well as $r$.

solution: The column $p \wedge q$ is true only in the two rows where $p$ and $q$ are both true, namely $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$ and $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F})$. The column $r$ is true in the four rows $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$ and $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T})$. The disjunction is true in any row belonging to either list. The row $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T})$ appears in both lists, so the total is $2 + 4 - 1 = 5$. The three false rows are $(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F})$, $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{F})$ and $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F})$.
formula_principle: A disjunction is true in every row where at least one of its two parts is true.
common_misconception: The student adds the true rows of the two parts without removing the rows counted twice.

subtopic: Building a truth table for a pattern in three variables
concept_tested: Recovering an assignment of three truth values from a stated truth value of the pattern
stem: For the statements $p$, $q$ and $r$, the statement pattern $(p \vee q) \rightarrow r$ is false. The truth values of $p$, $q$ and $r$ respectively can be

distractor_rationale.A: The student overlooks that a false antecedent makes the conditional true.
distractor_rationale.B: The student makes the consequent false and the antecedent true the wrong way round.
distractor_rationale.D: The student thinks a conditional is false whenever all three parts are true.

solution: For $(p \vee q) \rightarrow r$ to be false the antecedent $p \vee q$ must be true and the consequent $r$ must be false. So $r$ is false, and at least one of $p$ and $q$ is true. Checking the four given assignments: with $p$ true, $q$ false, $r$ false the antecedent is $\mathbf{T} \vee \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{T}$ and the pattern is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$, as required. With all three false the antecedent is $\mathbf{F}$ and the pattern is $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{T}$. With $p$ false, $q$ false, $r$ true the pattern is $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$. With all three true the pattern is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$.
formula_principle: A conditional is false only when its antecedent is $\mathbf{T}$ and its consequent is $\mathbf{F}$; work backwards from that single row.
common_misconception: The student sets every component to false in order to make the pattern false, ignoring the vacuous truth row.

subtopic: Tautology: recognising one and proving a pattern is one
concept_tested: Recognising the tautology built from a statement and its negation
stem: Which of the following statement patterns is a tautology?

distractor_rationale.B: The student confuses the pattern that is always false with the one that is always true.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes a conditional whose two parts are negations of each other must be true in every row.
distractor_rationale.D: The student overlooks the row in which $p$ is false.

solution: Take the two rows $p$ true and $p$ false. For $p \vee \sim p$: $\mathbf{T} \vee \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{F} \vee \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$, so it is $\mathbf{T}$ in both rows and is a tautology. For $p \wedge \sim p$: $\mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F} \wedge \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{F}$, a contradiction. For $p \leftrightarrow \sim p$: $\mathbf{T} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{F}$, also a contradiction. For $\sim p \rightarrow p$: with $p$ true it is $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$, but with $p$ false it is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$, so it is not a tautology.
formula_principle: A statement pattern is a tautology when the entry in its last column is $\mathbf{T}$ in every row.
common_misconception: The student mixes up the pattern that is always true, written $\mathbf{t}$, with the pattern that is always false, written $\mathbf{c}$.

subtopic: Tautology: recognising one and proving a pattern is one
concept_tested: Separating a valid implication pattern from three that fail in a single row
stem: Each of the following statement patterns is built from the statements $p$ and $q$. Which one carries the entry $\mathbf{T}$ in every row of its truth table?

distractor_rationale.A: The student treats a disjunction as though it guaranteed each of its parts.
distractor_rationale.B: The student treats one true part as enough to make a conjunction true.
distractor_rationale.C: The student detaches the consequent without checking that the antecedent holds.

solution: For $(p \wedge q) \rightarrow p$: the antecedent $p \wedge q$ is true only in the row $p$ true and $q$ true, and there the consequent $p$ is true, so the conditional is $\mathbf{T}$ there; in the other three rows the antecedent is false, so the conditional is $\mathbf{T}$ automatically. Hence all four rows carry $\mathbf{T}$. For $(p \vee q) \rightarrow p$: with $p$ false and $q$ true it is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$. For $p \rightarrow (p \wedge q)$: with $p$ true and $q$ false it is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$. For $(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow q$: with $p$ false and $q$ false it is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: To disprove a tautology it is enough to exhibit one row carrying $\mathbf{F}$; to prove one, every row must carry $\mathbf{T}$.
common_misconception: The student judges a pattern to be a tautology because it sounds reasonable, without testing the rows in which the antecedent is true.

subtopic: Tautology: recognising one and proving a pattern is one
concept_tested: Proving a tautology by testing only the rows in which the antecedent is true
stem: Exactly one of the following statement patterns is a tautology. Which one is it?

distractor_rationale.B: The student assumes the consequent of a conditional forces its antecedent.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes a false antecedent forces a false consequent.
distractor_rationale.D: The student assumes a disjunction rules out its second part once the first holds.

solution: For $[(p \rightarrow q) \wedge p] \rightarrow q$ the antecedent is true only when $p$ is true and $p \rightarrow q$ is true, which forces $q$ true; in that row the consequent $q$ is true, so the conditional is $\mathbf{T}$, and in every other row the antecedent is false and the conditional is $\mathbf{T}$ as well. Hence all four rows carry $\mathbf{T}$. For $[(p \rightarrow q) \wedge q] \rightarrow p$ take $p$ false and $q$ true: the antecedent is $\mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$ and the consequent $p$ is false, giving $\mathbf{F}$. For $[(p \rightarrow q) \wedge \sim p] \rightarrow \sim q$ take $p$ false and $q$ true: the antecedent is $\mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$ and $\sim q$ is false, giving $\mathbf{F}$. For $[(p \vee q) \wedge p] \rightarrow \sim q$ take $p$ true and $q$ true: the antecedent is $\mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$ and $\sim q$ is false, giving $\mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: An outer conditional can only fail where its antecedent is $\mathbf{T}$, so it is enough to examine those rows.
common_misconception: The student reasons from the true antecedent of a conditional backwards and concludes that the antecedent of the inner conditional must hold.

subtopic: Contradiction
concept_tested: MC14: Recognising and proving a contradiction
stem: A statement pattern whose truth value is $\mathbf{F}$ for every possible combination of truth values of its component statements is called

distractor_rationale.A: Student swaps the all-$\mathbf{F}$ definition with the all-$\mathbf{T}$ definition.
distractor_rationale.C: Student thinks any pattern that is not a tautology must be a contingency, forgetting the all-$\mathbf{F}$ case.
distractor_rationale.D: Student confuses the classification of a pattern with the operation of forming its dual.

solution: By definition, a pattern that takes the value $\mathbf{T}$ in every row is a tautology $\mathbf{t}$, a pattern that takes the value $\mathbf{F}$ in every row is a contradiction $\mathbf{c}$, and a pattern that takes both values is a contingency. The description given here is an entirely $\mathbf{F}$ column, so the pattern is a contradiction.
formula_principle: A statement pattern is a contradiction, written $\mathbf{c}$, when its last truth-table column contains $\mathbf{F}$ in every row.
common_misconception: Students memorise the two extreme definitions as a pair and attach the wrong name to the all-$\mathbf{F}$ column.

concept_tested: MC14: Recognising and proving a contradiction
stem: Which of the following statement patterns in $p$ and $q$ is a contradiction?

distractor_rationale.B: Student stops at the $\mathbf{TT}$ and $\mathbf{FF}$ rows, where this is $\mathbf{F}$, and never tests the mixed rows where it is $\mathbf{T}$.
distractor_rationale.C: Student sees a conditional with a stronger antecedent than consequent and calls it false, when it is in fact a tautology.

Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. The column is $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}$, so the pattern is a contradiction. subtopic: Contradiction
concept_tested: MC14: Recognising and proving a contradiction
stem: For the statement pattern $[(p \rightarrow q) \wedge p] \wedge \sim q$, the entries of the last column of the truth table, taken for $(p, q)$ equal to $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$, $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$ and $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$ in that order, are

distractor_rationale.A: Student builds the column of $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge p$ and then omits the factor $\sim q$.
distractor_rationale.C: Student reads the row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$, where $p \rightarrow q = \mathbf{F}$, as satisfying the bracket.
distractor_rationale.D: Student reports the column of $\sim q$ alone.

solution: Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T})$: $p \rightarrow q = \mathbf{T}$, $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge p = \mathbf{T}$, $\sim q = \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$: $p \rightarrow q = \mathbf{F}$, bracket $= \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$: $p \rightarrow q = \mathbf{T}$, bracket $= \mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$: $p \rightarrow q = \mathbf{T}$, bracket $= \mathbf{F}$, whole $= \mathbf{F}$. The column is therefore $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}$, so the pattern is a contradiction.
formula_principle: If $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge p$ is $\mathbf{T}$, then $q$ is $\mathbf{T}$, so conjoining $\sim q$ forces $\mathbf{F}$.
common_misconception: Students evaluate the bracket correctly and then forget that the only row where it is $\mathbf{T}$ is exactly the row where $\sim q$ is $\mathbf{F}$.

subtopic: Contingency
concept_tested: MC15: Contingency
stem: For a contingency in two component statements $p$ and $q$, the number of rows carrying the truth value $\mathbf{T}$ in the last column can be

distractor_rationale.A: The student forgets that a count of $0$ or of $4$ would make the pattern a contradiction or a tautology.
distractor_rationale.C: The student states the counts that are excluded rather than those that are allowed.
distractor_rationale.D: The student assumes a contingency must be true in exactly half of the rows.

solution: With two component statements the table has $2^{2} = 4$ rows. A count of $4$ would make the pattern a tautology and a count of $0$ would make it a contradiction. Both are excluded, so the possible counts are $1$, $2$ and $3$.
formula_principle: A contingency is a pattern that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction, so its column has at least one $\mathbf{T}$ and at least one $\mathbf{F}$.

concept_tested: MC20: Absorption law
stem: By the absorption law, $p \vee (p \wedge q)$ is logically equivalent to

distractor_rationale.A: Student absorbs the wrong component and keeps the one inside the bracket.
distractor_rationale.C: Student applies the law in the wrong direction and keeps the bracket.
distractor_rationale.D: Student drops the inner conjunction sign and keeps both components.

solution: Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{T}$, so $p \vee (p \wedge q) = \mathbf{T}$, matching $p = \mathbf{T}$. Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$, so the pattern is $\mathbf{T} \vee \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{T}$, matching $p = \mathbf{T}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$: $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$, pattern is $\mathbf{F}$, matching $p = \mathbf{F}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$: pattern is $\mathbf{F}$, matching $p = \mathbf{F}$. The column is that of $p$.
formula_principle: Absorption laws: $p \vee (p \wedge q) \equiv p$ and $p \wedge (p \vee q) \equiv p$.
common_misconception: Students remember that absorption removes something but cannot say which component survives.

subtopic: Absorption Law
concept_tested: MC20: Absorption law
stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to the statement pattern $(p \wedge q) \vee [p \wedge (q \vee r)]$?

distractor_rationale.A: Student absorbs the larger term into the smaller one instead of the other way round.
distractor_rationale.B: Student applies absorption to $p$ alone and discards both $q$ and $r$.
distractor_rationale.C: Student interchanges the two connectives while collapsing the pattern.

solution: By the distributive law $(p \wedge q) \vee [p \wedge (q \vee r)] \equiv p \wedge [q \vee (q \vee r)]$. By associativity and idempotence $q \vee (q \vee r) \equiv (q \vee q) \vee r \equiv q \vee r$, so the pattern is $p \wedge (q \vee r)$. Row check at $p = \mathbf{T}$, $q = \mathbf{F}$, $r = \mathbf{T}$: the pattern is $\mathbf{F} \vee (\mathbf{T} \wedge \mathbf{T}) = \mathbf{T}$, while $p \wedge q = \mathbf{F}$. At $p = \mathbf{T}$, $q = \mathbf{F}$, $r = \mathbf{F}$: the pattern is $\mathbf{F}$, while $p$ alone is $\mathbf{T}$. At $p = \mathbf{F}$, $q = \mathbf{T}$, $r = \mathbf{T}$: the pattern is $\mathbf{F}$, while $p \vee (q \wedge r) = \mathbf{T}$.
formula_principle: $(p \wedge s_1) \vee (p \wedge s_2) \equiv p \wedge (s_1 \vee s_2)$, then absorption $q \vee (q \vee r) \equiv q \vee r$.
common_misconception: Students apply absorption in the wrong direction and retain the smaller of the two terms.

stem: A statement pattern logically equivalent to $p \rightarrow q$ is

subtopic: Conditional as a Disjunction
concept_tested: MC21: Rewriting a conditional as a disjunction
stem: The statement pattern $\sim q \rightarrow p$ can be rewritten as

distractor_rationale.A: Student negates both components after removing the arrow.
distractor_rationale.B: Student converts the conditional into a conjunction.
distractor_rationale.C: Student negates the consequent instead of removing the existing negation on the antecedent.

solution: $\sim q \rightarrow p \equiv \sim (\sim q) \vee p \equiv q \vee p \equiv p \vee q$. Row check. Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T})$: $\sim q = \mathbf{F}$, so the conditional is $\mathbf{T}$, and $p \vee q = \mathbf{T}$. Row $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$: $\sim q = \mathbf{T}$, conditional is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}$, and $p \vee q = \mathbf{T}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$: $\sim q = \mathbf{F}$, conditional is $\mathbf{T}$, and $p \vee q = \mathbf{T}$. Row $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$: $\sim q = \mathbf{T}$, conditional is $\mathbf{T} \rightarrow \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}$, and $p \vee q = \mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: $s_1 \rightarrow s_2 \equiv \sim s_1 \vee s_2$ with $s_1 = \sim q$ and $s_2 = p$, together with $\sim (\sim q) \equiv q$.
common_misconception: Students apply the rule mechanically and add a second negation to an antecedent that is already negated.

major_topic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
subtopic: Conditional as a Disjunction
concept_tested: MC21: Rewriting a conditional as a disjunction
stem: The statement pattern $p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r)$ is logically equivalent to

distractor_rationale.B: Student joins the two antecedents by a disjunction instead of a conjunction.
distractor_rationale.C: Student regroups the brackets as though the conditional were associative.
distractor_rationale.D: Student detaches $r$ from the arrow and conjoins it.

solution: Converting twice, $p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r) \equiv \sim p \vee (\sim q \vee r)$. By associativity this is $(\sim p \vee \sim q) \vee r$, and by De Morgan $\sim (p \wedge q) \vee r$, which is $(p \wedge q) \rightarrow r$. Both sides are $\mathbf{F}$ exactly on the single row $p = \mathbf{T}$, $q = \mathbf{T}$, $r = \mathbf{F}$. For $(p \vee q) \rightarrow r$ take $p = \mathbf{F}$, $q = \mathbf{T}$, $r = \mathbf{F}$, where the given pattern is $\mathbf{T}$ but this is $\mathbf{F}$. For $(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow r$ take $p = \mathbf{F}$, $q = \mathbf{F}$, $r = \mathbf{F}$, where the given pattern is $\mathbf{T}$ but this is $\mathbf{F}$. For $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge r$ the same row gives $\mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: $p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r) \equiv \sim p \vee (\sim q \vee r) \equiv \sim (p \wedge q) \vee r \equiv (p \wedge q) \rightarrow r$.
common_misconception: Students treat the conditional as associative and regroup the brackets freely.

major_topic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
subtopic: Biconditional in Terms of Conditionals
concept_tested: MC22: Rewriting a biconditional using conditionals
stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to the statement pattern $p \leftrightarrow q$?

distractor_rationale.A: Student joins the two conditionals by a disjunction, which produces a tautology.
distractor_rationale.C: Student pairs the conditional with its contrapositive, which only repeats $p \rightarrow q$.
distractor_rationale.D: Student joins the two conditionals by another arrow instead of a conjunction.

solution: $p \leftrightarrow q$ has the column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$ over the rows $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F})$, $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T})$, $(\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F})$. $p \rightarrow q$ has the column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$ and $q \rightarrow p$ has the column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$. Their conjunction is $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$, which matches. Their disjunction is $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$, a tautology. Since $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p \equiv p \rightarrow q$, the pattern $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge (\sim q \rightarrow \sim p)$ reduces to $p \rightarrow q$, with column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$. The pattern $(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow (q \rightarrow p)$ has column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$.
formula_principle: $p \leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \rightarrow q) \wedge (q \rightarrow p)$.
common_misconception: Students remember that the biconditional splits into two conditionals but join them by the wrong connective.

subtopic: Biconditional in Terms of Conditionals
concept_tested: MC22: Rewriting a biconditional using conditionals
stem: Written with a single connective, the statement pattern $(\sim p \vee q) \wedge (\sim q \vee p)$ is

distractor_rationale.A: Student keeps only the row in which both components are true.
distractor_rationale.B: Student reads the two inner disjunctions as producing a single disjunction.
distractor_rationale.C: Student takes the pattern to be true exactly when $p$ and $q$ differ.

solution: The first bracket is $p \rightarrow q$ with column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$ and the second is $q \rightarrow p$ with column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$. The conjunction has column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$, which is the column of $p \leftrightarrow q$. Note that $p \wedge q$ has column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}$, $p \vee q$ has column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}$ and $p \veebar q$ has column $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: $\sim p \vee q \equiv p \rightarrow q$ and $\sim q \vee p \equiv q \rightarrow p$, so the conjunction is $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge (q \rightarrow p) \equiv p \leftrightarrow q$.
common_misconception: Students recognise each bracket as a conditional but do not recall that a conditional together with its converse is the biconditional.

concept_tested: MC23: Universal and existential quantifiers
stem: The symbolic form of the statement 'There exists a natural number $x$ for which $x + 4 = 9$' is

distractor_rationale.A: Student uses the universal quantifier for the phrase 'there exists'.
distractor_rationale.B: Student attaches the correct quantifier to the negated open sentence.
distractor_rationale.C: Student changes both the quantifier and the open sentence.

solution: The phrase 'there exists a natural number $x$' restricts $x$ to $\mathbb{N}$ and asserts that at least one such $x$ satisfies the open sentence $x + 4 = 9$. This is written $\exists x \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x + 4 = 9$. The open sentence itself is copied unchanged, so no $\ne$ appears. The statement is true, since $x = 5$ works.
formula_principle: 'There exists' is the existential quantifier $\exists$ and 'for all' is the universal quantifier $\forall$.
common_misconception: Students treat the two quantifier symbols as interchangeable and pick whichever appears first in their notes.

concept_tested: MC23: Universal and existential quantifiers
stem: Which of the following statements is quantified by the universal quantifier $\forall$?

distractor_rationale.A: Student reads 'there exists' as a claim about every element.
distractor_rationale.B: Student treats the word 'some' as a universal claim.
distractor_rationale.D: Student treats the phrase 'at least one' as a universal claim.

solution: 'For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x^2 \ge 0$' asserts the open sentence for each element of $\mathbb{R}$ without exception, so it carries $\forall$. The remaining three statements each assert only that the open sentence holds for at least one element, expressed as 'there exists', 'some' and 'at least one', so each carries $\exists$.
formula_principle: The universal quantifier $\forall$ corresponds to 'for all', 'for every' and 'each', while $\exists$ corresponds to 'there exists', 'some' and 'at least one'.
common_misconception: Students identify the quantifier from the mathematical content rather than from the words 'every', 'some' and 'at least one'.

concept_tested: MC24: Truth value of a quantified statement over a stated set
stem: Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. Which of the following statements has truth value $\mathbf{T}$?

distractor_rationale.A: Student verifies one element and then reads the universal quantifier as satisfied.
distractor_rationale.C: Student checks only the larger members of $S$ and ignores $x = 1$, $2$ and $3$.
distractor_rationale.D: Student accepts a value between two members of $S$ as though it were a member.

solution: For the first statement, $x = 5$ gives $5 + 3 = 8$, so at least one member works and the statement is true. For the second, $x = 1$ gives $4 \ne 8$, so it fails. For the third, $x = 1$ gives $1 > 3$, which is false. For the fourth, the squares of the members are $1$, $4$, $9$, $16$ and $25$, none of which equals $10$.
formula_principle: An existential statement is true if the open sentence holds for at least one member of the set; a universal statement is true only if it holds for every member.
common_misconception: Students accept a universal statement after confirming the open sentence for a single convenient member of the set.

concept_tested: MC24: Truth value of a quantified statement over a stated set
stem: Let $S = \{2, 3, 4, 5\}$, let $p$ be the statement '$\forall x \in S$, $x$ is a prime number' and let $q$ be the statement '$\exists x \in S$ such that $x + 3 = 7$'. The truth values of $p$ and $q$ respectively are

distractor_rationale.A: Student overlooks that $4$ is a member of $S$ and is not prime.
distractor_rationale.C: Student solves $x + 3 = 7$ but does not check that the root $4$ lies in $S$.
distractor_rationale.D: Student misjudges both statements, treating every member of $S$ as prime and rejecting the root $4$.

solution: For $p$, the members of $S$ are $2$, $3$, $4$ and $5$. Here $2$, $3$ and $5$ are prime but $4 = 2 \times 2$ is not, so the universal statement fails and $p$ has truth value $\mathbf{F}$. For $q$, solving $x + 3 = 7$ gives $x = 4$, and $4 \in S$, so at least one member satisfies the open sentence and $q$ has truth value $\mathbf{T}$.
formula_principle: Evaluate a universal statement by testing every member of the stated set and an existential statement by producing one member that works.
common_misconception: Students judge a universal statement over a listed set without testing every listed member.

subtopic: Negation of a Quantified Statement
concept_tested: MC25: Negation of a quantified statement
stem: For an open sentence $p(x)$ over a set $S$, the negation of '$\forall x \in S,\ p(x)$' is

options.D: $\forall x \in S,\ p(x)$ is false for no $x$

distractor_rationale.B: Student negates the open sentence but keeps the universal quantifier, which asserts that no element works.
distractor_rationale.C: Student changes the quantifier but leaves the open sentence un-negated.
distractor_rationale.D: Student writes a paraphrase that repeats the original claim instead of denying it.

solution: A universal statement claims that $p(x)$ holds for every member of $S$. To deny it, it is enough that $p(x)$ fails for at least one member. So both the quantifier and the open sentence change: $\forall$ becomes $\exists$ and $p(x)$ becomes $\sim p(x)$.

common_misconception: Students negate the open sentence but leave the quantifier alone, turning 'not all' into the much stronger 'none'.

stem: Let $S$ be the set of all the students in a class. Expressed in words, the negation of '$\forall x \in S$, $x$ has passed the examination' is

options.A: No student in the class has passed the examination
options.B: All the students in the class have not passed the examination
options.C: Some students in the class have not passed the examination
options.D: Some students in the class have passed the examination

distractor_rationale.B: Student negates the predicate only and keeps the word 'all'.
distractor_rationale.D: Student changes the quantifier only and leaves the predicate un-negated.

stem: The negation of the statement '$\exists x \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x^2 = 5$' is

concept_tested: MC25: Negation of a quantified statement
stem: Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. For the statement '$\forall x \in S,\ x + 3 < 9$', the negation and the truth value of that negation are

options.A: $\exists x \in S$ such that $x + 3 \ge 9$, with truth value $\mathbf{F}$
options.B: $\exists x \in S$ such that $x + 3 \ge 9$, with truth value $\mathbf{T}$
options.C: $\forall x \in S,\ x + 3 \ge 9$, with truth value $\mathbf{F}$
options.D: $\forall x \in S,\ x + 3 \ge 9$, with truth value $\mathbf{T}$

correct_answer_text: $\exists x \in S$ such that $x + 3 \ge 9$, with truth value $\mathbf{F}$

distractor_rationale.B: Student forms the negation correctly but evaluates the original statement as false, taking $x = 5$ to give $9 < 9$.
distractor_rationale.C: Student negates the open sentence but keeps the universal quantifier.
distractor_rationale.D: Student keeps the universal quantifier and also misjudges the truth value.

solution: The negation of $x + 3 < 9$ is $x + 3 \ge 9$, and the universal quantifier becomes existential, so the negation is $\exists x \in S$ such that $x + 3 \ge 9$. To find its truth value, test each member of $S$: $1 + 3 = 4$, $2 + 3 = 5$, $3 + 3 = 6$, $4 + 3 = 7$ and $5 + 3 = 8$. Every value is less than $9$, so no member satisfies $x + 3 \ge 9$ and the negation has truth value $\mathbf{F}$. Consistently, the original universal statement is true.
formula_principle: $\sim [\forall x \in S,\ p(x)] \equiv \exists x \in S$ such that $\sim p(x)$, and $\sim (a < b)$ is $a \ge b$.
common_misconception: Students form the negation correctly but then evaluate the negation on the boundary member as though $8 \ge 9$ were true.

solution: Apply De Morgan's law to the outer bracket: $\sim [p \wedge (\sim q \vee \sim r)] \equiv \sim p \vee \sim (\sim q \vee \sim r)$. common_misconception: Students apply De Morgan's law once to the outer bracket and stop, leaving the inner disjunction unchanged.

stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to the statement pattern $\sim (p \leftrightarrow q)$?

formula_principle: $\sim (p \leftrightarrow q) \equiv (p \wedge \sim q) \vee (q \wedge \sim p)$.
common_misconception: Students recall the two disagreement cases but join them by 'and', which can never be satisfied simultaneously.

solution: The converse of $p \rightarrow \sim q$ is $S: \sim q \rightarrow p$. Then $\sim S \equiv \sim q \wedge \sim p$, that is $\sim p \wedge \sim q$. A truth table over the four rows gives the column $\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{F}, \mathbf{T}$ for both $\sim S$ and $\sim p \wedge \sim q$.
formula_principle: Converse of $p \rightarrow q$ is $q \rightarrow p$, and $\sim (a \rightarrow b) \equiv a \wedge \sim b$.

concept_tested: Reading a circuit pattern combined with the test for a tautology
stem: Two switches are arranged so that the symbolic form of the resulting circuit is $(\sim p \vee q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)$. This circuit is

options.A: always on, whatever the positions of the two switches
options.B: always off, whatever the positions of the two switches
options.C: on only when both the switches are closed
options.D: on only when exactly one of the switches is closed

correct_answer_text: always on, whatever the positions of the two switches

distractor_rationale.B: The student mistakes the pattern for a contradiction.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads only the second block of the pattern.
distractor_rationale.D: The student reads the pattern as an exclusive disjunction.

solution: The first block is $\sim p \vee q$, which is $p \rightarrow q$. The second block is $p \wedge \sim q$, which is exactly $\sim (p \rightarrow q)$. Their disjunction is of the form $X \vee \sim X$ and is therefore a tautology $\mathbf{t}$, with the column $\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{T}$. A circuit whose symbolic form is a tautology is always on.
formula_principle: $\sim p \vee q \equiv p \rightarrow q$ and $p \wedge \sim q \equiv \sim (p \rightarrow q)$, so the pattern is of the form $X \vee \sim X \equiv \mathbf{t}$.
common_misconception: Students test one or two rows only and conclude that some arrangement of the switches breaks the circuit.

concept_tested: Composition of the inverse and the contrapositive of a conditional
stem: The contrapositive of the inverse of the statement pattern $p \rightarrow q$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student assumes that applying two operations returns the original conditional.
distractor_rationale.B: The student negates the inverse instead of taking its contrapositive.
distractor_rationale.D: The student negates the antecedent of the inverse only.

solution: The inverse is $\sim p \rightarrow \sim q$. Its contrapositive negates both parts and interchanges them: $\sim(\sim q) \rightarrow \sim(\sim p)$, which simplifies to $q \rightarrow p$. This is the converse of the original conditional, which is consistent with the fact that the converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other.
formula_principle: Inverse of $p \rightarrow q$ is $\sim p \rightarrow \sim q$; the contrapositive of $a \rightarrow b$ is $\sim b \rightarrow \sim a$.
common_misconception: Students believe that a contrapositive applied to an inverse cancels out and returns the original conditional.

concept_tested: Simplification of a circuit pattern combined with the identification of a tautology
stem: The simplified form of the statement pattern $[p \wedge (q \vee \sim q)] \vee [\sim p \wedge (r \vee \sim r)]$, which represents a switching circuit, is

distractor_rationale.A: The student reduces each bracket to a contradiction instead of a tautology.
distractor_rationale.B: The student cancels the complementary pairs but keeps one switch from each bracket.
distractor_rationale.D: The student keeps every switch in the circuit instead of simplifying the two bracketed blocks.

solution: Inside the first bracket $q \vee \sim q \equiv \mathbf{t}$, so the block becomes $p \wedge \mathbf{t} \equiv p$. Inside the second bracket $r \vee \sim r \equiv \mathbf{t}$, so that block becomes $\sim p \wedge \mathbf{t} \equiv \sim p$. The pattern is therefore $p \vee \sim p \equiv \mathbf{t}$, and the circuit is always on. Its column is $\mathbf{T}$ in all eight rows.
formula_principle: $q \vee \sim q \equiv \mathbf{t}$, $X \wedge \mathbf{t} \equiv X$ and $p \vee \sim p \equiv \mathbf{t}$.
common_misconception: Students simplify the inner brackets correctly but then join the two remaining blocks by a conjunction, because the original brackets both contained a conjunction.

concept_tested: Contrapositive of a conditional stated using a necessary condition about circuits
stem: Consider the statement "A necessary condition for a switching circuit to be always on is that its symbolic form is a tautology". Its contrapositive is

options.A: If the symbolic form of a switching circuit is not a tautology, then the circuit is always on.
options.B: If the symbolic form of a switching circuit is a tautology, then the circuit is always on.
options.C: A switching circuit is always on and its symbolic form is not a tautology.
options.D: If the symbolic form of a switching circuit is not a tautology, then the circuit is not always on.

correct_answer_text: If the symbolic form of a switching circuit is not a tautology, then the circuit is not always on.

distractor_rationale.A: The student negates the first part of the converse and leaves the second part unnegated.
distractor_rationale.B: Converse of the intended statement.
distractor_rationale.C: The student negates the conditional instead of forming its contrapositive.

solution: The necessary condition is the consequent. With $p$: a switching circuit is always on and $q$: its symbolic form is a tautology, the statement is $p \rightarrow q$. The contrapositive $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$ reads: if the symbolic form of a switching circuit is not a tautology, then the circuit is not always on.
formula_principle: \"$q$ is necessary for $p$\" means $p \rightarrow q$; the contrapositive of $p \rightarrow q$ is $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$.
common_misconception: The connector used is "necessary condition"; students place it in the antecedent, which turns the intended statement into its converse before the contrapositive is even formed.

subtopic: Mixed Concepts of Mathematical Logic
concept_tested: Reverse reasoning on the condition for a circuit to be always on
stem: A switching circuit has the symbolic form $(p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \vee s$, where the switch $s$ is still to be chosen. For the current to flow for every arrangement of the switches $p$ and $q$, the statement $s$ must be

distractor_rationale.A: The student repeats the statement that survives the simplification instead of its negation.
distractor_rationale.B: The student chooses the switch that cancels out during the simplification.
distractor_rationale.C: The student negates the switch that cancels out instead of the one that survives.

solution: The first two blocks give $(p \vee \sim p) \wedge q$, which is $\mathbf{t} \wedge q$, that is $q$. The circuit is therefore $q \vee s$. This is a tautology for every arrangement only when $s \equiv \sim q$, since $q \vee \sim q \equiv \mathbf{t}$. Any of the other choices leaves at least one row false: with $s$ as $p$, the row in which $p$ is $\mathbf{F}$ and $q$ is $\mathbf{F}$ gives $\mathbf{F}$.
formula_principle: $(p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \equiv (p \vee \sim p) \wedge q \equiv q$, and a circuit is always on when its pattern is $\mathbf{t}$, for which $q \vee \sim q$ is needed.
common_misconception: Students simplify only the first block and then choose a switch that makes that block, rather than the whole circuit, always closed.
